idiom_name: function-pointer dispatch table + atomic snapshot swap (dlopen for hot-swapped rule modules)
implementation_notes: C has no router abstraction, so the rule base is a hand-built array or struct of conditions and function pointers and the control channel is whatever the process accepts as a reload (SIGHUP, a control thread reading a file, or a dlopen'ed rule module). Publish the table as one pointer-sized value and swap it with the C11 <stdatomic.h> primitives, or a mutex where the runtime lacks them, so no reader can observe a partially built table; dlopen/dlsym lets the evaluator itself be replaced as a shared object, but the handler signature must be fixed and the module must outlive every table that references it. Keep the classic structure only when hot rule replacement is genuinely required - a table regenerated at build time is simpler and faster when the rules are stable.
pitfalls: Freeing the replaced table right after the swap is a use-after-free: a reader may still be dispatching on that snapshot - retire it after a grace period or never free it.

Function pointers carry no per-rule state, so a rule needing a queue handle or connection smuggles it through a global or context pointer, which is where the thread-safety of the rule base usually breaks.
Without an atomic or compiler barrier the load can be hoisted out of the message loop, so a published rule edit never becomes visible.
